ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The left figure is a triangular piece of paper, and the dashed line indicates the crease; the right figure shows that the shape after folding is a heptagon, with several gray shaded regions and a middle white unshaded region in the figure, and the dashed line also marks the position of the part that was flipped over before folding. According to the right figure, after folding it can be regarded as the union of the part on one side of the original crease and the other part that was folded over; the middle white region is the part where two layers of paper overlap, and the gray shaded regions are the parts covered by only one layer of paper. Reasoning: Let the area of the original triangle be T, the area of the heptagon after folding be H, and the area of the two-layer overlapping part be O. Folding does not change the total area of the paper, so the total area counted by number of layers is still T. The heptagon is the union of the two parts after folding, therefore H = T - O. The shaded part is the region covered by only one layer, and its area is the total paper area minus the two-layer area repeatedly counted in the overlapping region, namely S = T - 2O. The problem gives S = 1, and T = 1.5H = 3H/2. Substituting H = T - O gives T = (3/2)(T - O), so 2T = 3T - 3O, hence O = T/3. Thus S = T - 2(T/3) = T/3. Since S = 1, T/3 = 1, obtaining T = 3.

raw_record.question_text: A triangular piece of paper is folded along the dotted line shown in the left-hand diagram to form the heptagon shown in the right-hand diagram. The total area of the shaded parts of the heptagon is $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$. The area of the original triangle is $1 \frac{1}{2}$ times the area of the heptagon. What is the area of the original triangle, in $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$?

method.method_draft: First read the right-hand diagram as a union of two congruent-to-original pieces after folding: the original right-side portion of the triangle and the reflected left triangular flap. The central unshaded polygon is the overlap of these two layers, while the shaded regions are exactly the parts covered by only one layer. Let the original triangle area be T, the heptagon area be H, and the overlap area be O. Folding preserves paper area, so before accounting for overlap the two pieces have total area T. The visible heptagon is their union, so H = T - O. The shaded single-layer area is the symmetric-difference area, so S = T - 2O. From the text, S = 1 and T = 1.5H. Substitute H = T - O into T = 1.5H to get O = T/3. Then S = T - 2(T/3) = T/3. Since S = 1, T = 3.

Folding does not change the total area of the paper, so the total area counted by number of layers is still T. The heptagon is the union of the two parts after folding, therefore H = T - O. The shaded part is the region covered by only one layer, and its area is the total paper area minus the two-layer area repeatedly counted in the overlapping region, namely S = T - 2O. The problem gives S = 1, and T = 1.5H = 3H/2. Substituting H = T - O gives T = (3/2)(T - O), so 2T = 3T - 3O, hence O = T/3. Thus S = T - 2(T/3) = T/3. Since S = 1, T/3 = 1, obtaining T = 3.
